$comment: Declared unreachable surfaces, with a WRITTEN REASON for each. Enforced by
tools/check_reachability.py (CI job 'Reachability - nothing implemented-and-uncalled').
Unreachable is sometimes exactly correct: a capability-denied command MUST have no caller,
and a superseded sibling legitimately outlives its last call site. What hides a defect is
unreachable-AND-undeclared - the state in which nobody can tell which of those it is. So
this file is the point of the gate, not an escape hatch from it: every entry costs a
sentence that a reviewer can disagree with, and 'unreachable, no reason given' is refused
by the gate itself (see MIN_REASON_CHARS / PLACEHOLDER_REASONS).
Adding an entry is a claim. If the command later gains a real caller, the gate turns RED
and asks you to DELETE the entry - deliberately, so an exception cannot silently outlive
the condition it described.
`rust_symbols` covers apps/desktop/src-tauri/** the same way `engine_symbols` covers the
python engine. It needs `module` as well as `defined_in`, because a Rust caller must NAME
the symbol (`module::name(`): a bare-name scan would count any unrelated function of the
same name as a caller, and names like `create_schema` / `resolve` / `sweep` are shared by
half a dozen sibling modules in brops-core. rustc never warns about an uncalled `pub fn`
in a library crate, which is why this whole class was invisible here until 2026-08-09.
`rust_symbols` is NO LONGER EMPTY as of 2026-08-10: it holds the SIX halves of one open gap -
the rev-30 4.10(f) DESKTOP output pull (governed_output_pull::pull_output, ai::governed_pull_output,
ai::governed_turn_output_read) and the rev-30 4.6 result frame that would deliver its capability
token (governed_bridge_result::parse, ::parse_frame, ::check_echoes). Read their reasons together -
they describe ONE gap, not six, and the gap MOVED on 2026-08-10: it used to be 'no 4.6 frame on
either hop'; 4.6 now exists on both, and what is missing is 4.10(g)'s
`bridge.governed-turn-submit.v1` - the hop that would make a sidecar hold a 4.10(e) reply to
re-frame in the first place. The section previously held governed_output_stream::
4.10(e) `signed` frame producer, not three. The section previously held governed_output_stream::
mint/resolve/sweep, whose own declaration said 'wiring a caller is a rewrite, not a hookup, and
stream_binding_mismatch cannot be produced at all'. That turned out to be the whole finding, and
the module was DELETED on 2026-08-10 when 4.10(f) was built as SUPERVISOR state (Appendix B puts
governed_output_streams in the 0700 supervisor-only DB, not the broker DB the Rust module used).
It could not have been left: its `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS governed_output_streams` ran on the
same rusqlite connection one line before supervisor_ledger::create_schema in all four call sites,
so keeping it would have made the canonical DDL a silent no-op and the divergent table the one
that actually existed. The gate is what forced that choice to be visible: `defined_in` must
exist, so a declaration cannot outlive the file it describes.
Reasons: capability-denied | superseded | governed-wall | backend-only | not-yet-wired.
'not-yet-wired' is an honest OPEN gap and must name where it is tracked.
Observed state recorded 2026-08-07 on branch wave/phase-push-1; the gate re-derives it on
every run rather than trusting these notes.

decide_approval.note: The generic approve verb is DENIED to the main window in capabilities/default.json (deny-decide-approval, T-011): approving must require a renderer-independent native confirmation, so a compromised webview cannot approve anything. Having no caller is the ENFORCED state, not an oversight - apps/desktop/src/features/approvalsAuthority.ts names it only as DENIED_DECIDE_COMMAND, a constant that exists so the page can assert it never renders a control for it. The reachable approve path is confirm_approval; the fail-safe path is reject_approval.
decide_approval.observed: 2026-08-07: no invoke; one non-call mention as DENIED_DECIDE_COMMAND in features/approvalsAuthority.ts.

post_message.note: Superseded by post_user_message for every renderer path (P1-6): post_user_message fixes the role server-side, so the webview cannot choose it, while post_message only VALIDATES the role against WEBVIEW_MESSAGE_ROLES = ["user"]. services/desktop.ts exposes postMessage(), which invokes post_user_message. post_message is therefore the WIDER of the two - it accepts a role and checks it, where the superseding command never lets the webview name one at all - and it stays registered and allow-granted with nothing calling it. That is residual invokable surface with no user; flipping its grant to deny is the cheapest way to remove it, and the gate will say so again the moment anyone wonders.
post_message.observed: 2026-08-07: zero invocations anywhere under apps/desktop/src/**, production or test.

reply_in_conversation.note: The non-streaming twin of stream_reply: same context assembly, same one-time-challenge -> governed_turn -> verify_and_record_receipt pipeline, differing only in delivery. Every chat surface uses the streaming sibling (services/desktop.ts streamReply), so the buffered variant has no frontend wrapper. It is kept because the governed pipeline it carries is the same audited one and a non-streaming caller (automation, a headless turn) is a plausible future consumer; until such a caller exists it is unreached by design.
reply_in_conversation.observed: 2026-08-07: zero invocations under apps/desktop/src/**; commands.rs keeps it on the governed path.

set_run_step_status.note: No surface authors a run-step status directly. Command.tsx drives steps through stream_run_step (the governed execution path, which sets status as a consequence of real work) and advance_run (which moves the run forward transactionally). A renderer that could stamp an arbitrary step status could claim a step succeeded without it having run, which is the exact honesty defect the six-surface work closed, so leaving this uncalled is the safer state.
set_run_step_status.observed: 2026-08-07: zero invocations under apps/desktop/src/**; add_run_step / advance_run / stream_run_step are the live callers of the run-step repo.

create_decision.note: An OPEN gap, declared rather than dressed up. The Decisions page is a read-only mirror today - it renders list_decisions plus the engine evidence-chain read - and offers no control that records a decision, so create_decision is registered and allow-granted with nothing invoking it. Two honest closures exist: wire a create control on the Decisions page, or flip the grant to deny because authoring governance decisions from the webview is not wanted. Until one is chosen this is invokable surface with no user.
create_decision.observed: 2026-08-07: zero invocations under apps/desktop/src/**; grant is allow-create-decision, policy tier L1.

assert_no_bytecode_shadow.reason: The worked example this gate was built around, and it CHANGED STATE while the gate was being written. Residual item O-1 (HIGH) is the canonical 'implemented and nothing calls it': the function exists, is documented, raises ProtectedScopeError for __pycache__/.pyc/.pyo under a digest root - and for the whole life of the repository had zero callers, so a forged .pyc could shadow a digest-verified .py and nothing noticed. It now has real callers on the wall's own path, so the expectation is must_have_caller and the gate protects those call sites: if either is refactored away the gate turns RED rather than the defect silently reopening. NOTE THE LIMIT - this proves the calls EXIST; it does not verify the rest of O-1 closure (hooks running python -B, compileall scoped off digest roots, the stray-.pyc regression test), and O-1's status in docs/PHASE_10_PRODUCTION_ITEMS.md is owned there, not here.
assert_no_bytecode_shadow.observed: 2026-08-07: two call sites in engine/runtime/bro_control_plane.py - line 80 in _bind_workspace (before any binding is loaded) and line 267 in the settlement path (a second process the binding path never covers). Both were UNCOMMITTED working-tree changes by a concurrent agent at the time of this run; the gate re-derives them every run, so a revert turns it RED.

head_anchor_payload.reason: The OWNER-FACING half of the anchor API. O-2's fix landed: `append` now assembles the anchor payload itself and refuses any document that is not a signature over exactly those bytes, via the private `_anchor_payload` this function also wraps. What stays caller-less in this repo is deliberate -- the caller is the owner's out-of-band signing command, reached through BRO_AUDIT_ANCHOR_SIGNER, and a key the ledger's own writer could reach would prove nothing. So this is an exported API with an external consumer, NOT dead code. It gains an in-repo caller only if a signing helper ships inside the engine, which would defeat the point.
head_anchor_payload.observed: 2026-08-07, after O-2 landed: zero call-shaped references outside bro_audit_log.py. The enforcement now lives in `append` + `verify(keys=...)`, which the gate does not track by name.

attach_head_anchor.reason: The install half of the same owner-facing API: it verifies a signed anchor against the trusted registry and against the ledger's current chain before storing it. Caller-less in this repo for the same reason as `head_anchor_payload` -- the party holding the signing key is outside the engine by design. Not dead code, and not the O-2 gap: that gap closed when `append` started attaching an anchor and keyed `verify` started requiring one.
attach_head_anchor.observed: 2026-08-07, after O-2 landed: zero call-shaped references outside bro_audit_log.py.

verify_conductor_session_token.reason: ENFORCED, not excused: this is the one of the five that genuinely has a caller, and the gate now protects that. If the call site is removed or refactored away the gate turns RED, because losing it would silently return conductor identity to a plain environment-variable claim.
verify_conductor_session_token.observed: 2026-08-07: called from engine/runtime/bro_completion.py (authorize_conductor_stop path), which also audit-logs the exemption.

require_conductor_session_token.reason: A policy KEY, not a function, so `defined_in` is null and the flag is 'called' by being read. It is read through the named constant CONDUCTOR_SESSION_POLICY_KEY rather than as a bare literal, so the declaration states that one hop and the gate verifies the binding is real before following it - an undeclared indirection would otherwise read as zero readers. IMPORTANT LIMIT, and the reason this entry is worth reading twice: the gate proves the flag is READ by the enforcement path and proves NOTHING about whether it is SET. That second half is residual item O-3 (MEDIUM), needs an operator-signed conductor-session artifact only the Owner can mint, and is outside this gate by construction.
require_conductor_session_token.observed: 2026-08-07: engine/runtime/bro_policy.py binds CONDUCTOR_SESSION_POLICY_KEY to the flag and reads it in conductor_session_token_required, which now treats an UNDECLARED requirement as a REQUIRED one (an uncommitted concurrent change - the previous code defaulted to False). Still absent from engine/.bro/policy.json.

pull_output.reason: The rev-30 4.10(f) DESKTOP pull loop: it drives the chunked read, reassembles into a bounded buffer, and applies the 4.6/7.1 whole-output length+digest gate against the SIGNED envelope (never 4.10(e)'s TRANSPORT-ONLY echo of the same two values). The pull needs an `output_stream_id`, and rev-30 4.10(f) permits exactly one source for it: the 4.10(e) `brops.governed-turn-result.v1` `signed` frame. That frame NOW HAS a supervisor-side producer - `engine/runtime/governed_acceptance.py::AcceptanceDriver`, which requires an OutputReadService and carries the minted token; it landed in this same tree from a concurrent change and was uncommitted when this entry was written, so read the citation as of that moment. 4.6's `bridge.governed-turn-result.v1` - the only frame that moves that token across the sidecar boundary - now EXISTS on both hops (2026-08-10): the re-framer in bridge/governed_turn_result_bridge.py and the strict parser in apps/desktop/src-tauri/core/src/governed_bridge_result.rs. What is still missing is one hop further out: 4.6 is the REPLY to 4.10(g)'s `bridge.governed-turn-submit.v1`, and 4.10(g) is NOT IMPLEMENTED - no submit branch in engine_sidecar._dispatch and no orchestrator that drives 4.10(a0)/(a)/(b)/(c)/(d) inside one one-shot subprocess - so nothing ever holds a 4.10(e) reply to re-frame, and wiring a caller today would still mean inventing a token, which is the single thing 4.10(f) says may never happen. The dependency is typed rather than described: `OutputStreamCapability` can only be built from a verified 4.9 envelope plus a 43-char token, so the day a 4.6 frame delivers one the compiler names every place it has to reach. A second, larger disagreement would survive fixing that: the broker's Linux execution (`broker/src/chain_executor.rs::LinuxGovernedExecution`) reads the recorder's output off the local filesystem with `std::fs::read(&report_path)` instead of through this egress at all, so even a delivered token would not by itself put the pull on the live path. This entry is deliberately the same shape as the one that held `governed_output_stream::mint/resolve/sweep` before that ladder was deleted, and it is NOT the same claim: that one said wiring a caller was 'a rewrite, not a hookup' and that one of its refusals could not be produced at all. Every gate here is produced by name from a reply a real supervisor can send, and the supervisor half it talks to is shipped and served. UPDATED 2026-08-10 (§4.10(g) sidecar half): the reason for this symbol being caller-less MOVED one hop further out and is now narrower than the text above describes. §4.10(g)'s sidecar orchestrator EXISTS — `bridge/governed_turn_submit.py`, reached from the `bridge.governed-turn-submit.v1` branch in `bridge/engine_sidecar.py::_dispatch` — and it drives §4.10(a0) → §4.10(a)(b)(c) → §4.10(d) inside one one-shot subprocess and re-frames the §4.10(e) reply into a §4.6 frame carrying a supervisor-minted `output_stream_id`, proven end to end against the real `OpenService`/`StagingService`/`EvidenceRequestService`, a real ledger and the real isolated signer in `engine/tests/test_governed_turn_submit_e2e.py`. So the sentence 'there is no submit branch and no orchestrator' above is HISTORY. What still blocks a caller is that nothing WRITES a submit frame: `prepare_governed_turn_v1b`, `PreparedGovernedTurnV1B`, `GovernedGenerationConfig`, `resolve_governed_generation_config_v1b` and `governed_turn_submit_prepared` return zero hits in a whole-tree grep, and the broker's one production `GovernedExecutor` (`broker/src/chain_executor.rs::ChainExecutor`) has a single `Command::new` and it is the recorder. A second blocker survives fixing that: the live supervisor (`engine/ci/live/run_supervisor.py`) constructs no `OpenService`/`StagingService`/`EvidenceRequestService`/`OutputReadService`, so its socket serves none of the five protocols the ladder speaks. The dependency stays TYPED rather than described, exactly as before.
